sections.body: SAR planning draws on decades of documented lost-person behavior data, and different categories of subjects behave in statistically distinct ways that change how a search is run. Young children, especially under about six, often do not respond to their name being called by searchers and may actively hide from strangers, including searchers themselves, out of fear or shyness — a team calling out and listening for a reply can walk right past a hidden child, which is why child searches emphasize visual sweeps and quiet listening for other sounds over shouted contact. Elderly subjects, and especially those with dementia or Alzheimer's-related cognitive impairment, are frequently found relatively close to their starting point, often following roads, fence lines, or other linear features rather than cutting cross-country, and can become disoriented in familiar areas they've lived in for decades — a pattern distinct from a healthy adult hiker who typically ranges farther and follows trail logic. Subjects with autism spectrum conditions are statistically drawn toward water, which shapes where teams prioritize their initial hasty search. None of this changes what a bystander should personally do in the moment — report immediately, give searchers as much specific detail as possible about the person's habits and condition — but it explains why search planners ask pointed questions about age, cognitive status, and known behavioral patterns rather than treating every missing-person case identically.

sections.heading: What Happens When They Find You
sections.body: If you hear or see search activity — an aircraft, a dog team, voices calling out — respond immediately and as visibly as possible rather than waiting to be sure, since search teams are actively scanning and a missed window can mean they move on to the next segment. Shout, blow a whistle in bursts of three, wave brightly colored clothing or gear, and if you have a signal mirror, flash it toward aircraft or distant search parties — the specific techniques for each of these are covered in the Signalling for Rescue guide. Once contact is made, a searcher will typically assess you for injuries and medical needs before anything else, radio your location and status back to the incident command post using a grid reference or coordinates, and only then begin coordinating the actual extraction — which might be walking out with an escort, a wheeled or carried litter evacuation for anyone who can't walk, or a helicopter hoist or landing zone extraction in more remote or hazardous terrain. Stay where you are once contact is made unless specifically told to move, since the team now has your exact location relayed to command and unplanned movement can complicate the extraction plan or separate you from your rescuers again. Expect a debrief afterward — searchers will ask what happened, what decisions you made, and what worked or didn't, both for your own medical and psychological follow-up and to improve how future searches for similar situations are run.

sections.heading: Building the Habits Before You Ever Need Rescuing
sections.body: Most of what makes a search fast happens before anyone is ever lost. File a real trip plan every time, not just for long or ambitious trips — a surprising share of searches start on short, familiar routes that went wrong in an ordinary way. Carry visible, high-contrast clothing or gear as a standard part of your kit, even if it isn't your style preference for everyday use — a bright rain shell or pack cover doubles as searchable equipment. Keep a phone charged and, in areas with poor coverage, consider a satellite messenger or personal locator beacon, which can transmit a GPS position and trigger a rescue response even with zero cell signal — covered in more depth in the Calling for Help guide. Learn your own area or trip's realistic hazards and checkpoints well enough that, if things go wrong, your instinct to stay put or self-extract is an informed decision rather than a guess made under stress. If you're part of a group, agree in advance on what happens if someone gets separated — a specific meeting point, a wait time, and who calls for help and when — so that decision isn't being made for the first time in the middle of an actual emergency, when clear thinking is hardest to come by.

guides.title: Improvised Rescue Rigging: Mechanical Advantage for Non-Technical Rescuers
guides.summary: Rope rescue is one of the fastest ways for a well-meaning bystander to become a second casualty. This guide explains low-angle versus high-angle situations, the basics of anchors and mechanical advantage, and exactly where the line sits between what an untrained person can safely attempt and what genuinely needs a trained team.

sections.heading: The First Rule: This Is Where Helpers Become Victims
sections.body: More rescuers are hurt or killed attempting technical rope rescue without training than in almost any other category of well-intentioned emergency response, and the reason is consistent: rope systems fail in ways that are invisible until they fail completely. A frayed core strand under a sheath, an anchor that looks solid but isn't rated for a sudden load, a knot tied slightly wrong, a system with no backup if the primary component lets go — all of these look identical to a correct setup right up until someone is falling. Trained rescue teams spend days of formal instruction and ongoing certification specifically on load calculations, anchor building, and backup redundancy before they're cleared to run a live rescue system, and even then, technical rope rescue accounts for a disproportionate share of on-duty rescuer injuries industry-wide. This guide is not a substitute for that training — it exists to help you recognize the difference between situations where a careful, simple, low-consequence assist is reasonable, and situations that genuinely require waiting for people who've done this before. If you take away one thing, take this: the instinct that says 'I can rig something and get them' has killed experienced climbers and outdoorspeople, not just novices, and the safest rescue is very often the one where you stay anchored, stay in contact, and wait.

sections.heading: Low-Angle vs. High-Angle: Know Which Situation You're In
sections.body: This distinction is the single most important filter for deciding what's reasonable to attempt. A low-angle situation is one where the slope is gentle enough — roughly under about 40 degrees as a rough rule of thumb, though it depends heavily on surface and footing — that a person could still walk or scramble on it unassisted if they weren't injured or exhausted, and where a rope, if used at all, functions mainly as a handline or safety backup rather than something someone's full body weight hangs from continuously. A high-angle situation is steep enough that a person's weight is genuinely suspended by the rope system — a cliff face, a vertical drop, an overhang, a crevasse — where a rope failure means a real, often fatal, fall with nothing to catch it. Low-angle assists — a handline for someone to steady themselves on a steep but walkable slope, a hasty belay where you're braced and simply providing a point to hold rather than bearing full weight — are within reach of a careful, prepared non-technical person using good judgment. High-angle rescue is a different category of risk entirely, requiring rated equipment, redundant anchors, load-tested systems, and specific technique, and is exactly the situation where waiting for a trained rope rescue or technical mountain rescue team is almost always the right call, even if it feels agonizingly slow.

sections.heading: Anchors: The Unglamorous Foundation
sections.body: Every rope system is only as trustworthy as the point it's anchored to, and anchor failure is one of the most common root causes in rope rescue accidents. A solid anchor needs to hold far more force than it looks like it should — a falling or swinging load generates dynamic force well beyond simple body weight, sometimes multiple times over, which is why anchors rated for static loads can still fail under a sudden jolt. Good natural anchors include large, clearly healthy trees with a solid root system, substantial rock features with no visible cracking, or solid structural members if you're working around a building or vehicle — never trust a small tree, a loose boulder, a fence post, or a vehicle bumper, all of which have failed in real incidents. Where possible, build a load-sharing anchor using two or more independent points connected so that if one fails, the load transfers to the other rather than dropping entirely — this is standard practice in trained rescue rigging and dramatically improves the margin of safety over a single point. Always keep the angle between anchor legs narrow rather than wide, since a wide angle between two anchor points multiplies the force each leg experiences rather than dividing it evenly. If you have any doubt about whether something can hold a person's full weight under a sudden load, it cannot — treat the anchor question as the one place where guessing is not acceptable.

sections.heading: What 2:1, 3:1, and 5:1 Mechanical Advantage Actually Mean
sections.body: Mechanical advantage in a haul system describes how much a pulley-and-line arrangement multiplies your pulling force, at the cost of having to pull proportionally more rope through your hands. A 2:1 system — a single pulley or fixed point at the load, with the rope running back to the hauler — roughly halves the force needed to move the load, but you have to pull two feet of rope for every one foot the load moves. A 3:1 system, commonly called a Z-drag or Z-rig for the zigzag shape the rope makes, theoretically triples pulling force by routing the rope through a pulley at the load and a friction hitch anchored back near the hauler, at the cost of pulling three feet of rope per foot of travel. Higher ratios like 5:1 or 6:1 are typically compound systems — a smaller mechanical advantage system hauling on the rope of a larger one — and while they multiply force further, they also multiply complexity, rope stretch, and friction losses correspondingly. In practice, real systems never deliver the full theoretical ratio: every pulley, carabiner, and direction change the rope passes through bleeds off some force to friction, and improvised hardware like a carabiner used in place of a proper pulley loses considerably more than a purpose-built pulley wheel does. This is why trained rescuers treat these ratios as rough guides for planning, not guarantees, and why simpler, lower-ratio systems that are easier to build correctly are often preferred over complex ones that are easier to get wrong.

sections.heading: Building a Basic Z-Drag (3:1 Haul)
sections.body: A Z-drag is one of the more commonly taught improvised haul systems specifically because it can be built from a single rope, a couple of pulleys or carabiners, and friction hitch cord, and it's genuinely useful for a low-angle assist such as helping someone up a steep bank or hauling light equipment. The basic layout runs the main rope from the anchor to the load, then back toward the hauler through a pulley or carabiner attached to the load, then through a second pulley attached to a friction hitch — a prusik or similar cord loop — clipped onto the standing part of the rope near the anchor. As the hauler pulls, the friction hitch slides forward, and when they release to reset their grip, the hitch grabs the rope and holds the progress made, functioning as a ratchet that stops the load from sliding back. This is precisely the kind of system that rewards careful, slow assembly and a walk-through before it's loaded: check that the friction hitch actually grips under tension and releases cleanly when unweighted, that the anchor is solid, and that everyone understands their role before any real weight goes on the line. A Z-drag built for a light-duty, low-angle assist with a conservative anchor and careful hitch-checking is reasonable for a prepared non-technical person; a Z-drag intended to lift a person's full weight vertically is not, and belongs to trained rope rescue technique.

sections.heading: Friction Hitches: The Rescuer's Safety Net
sections.body: A friction hitch is a loop of cord tied around a load-bearing rope in a way that grips tightly when weighted and slides freely when not — the prusik hitch is the classic example, along with variants like the klemheist and the autoblock, each with slightly different grip and release behavior. These hitches serve two distinct purposes in improvised rescue work: as the ratchet component in a haul system like the Z-drag described above, and as a personal safety backup, sometimes called a self-belay, that a person can attach between themselves and a fixed rope so that if they slip or lose control, the hitch grabs and arrests the fall rather than letting them slide the full length of the rope. A properly tied friction hitch needs cord noticeably thinner and typically of different material than the rope it's tied around — using cord too close in diameter or the same slippery material as the host rope can prevent it from gripping reliably, which defeats its entire purpose. Test any friction hitch by weighting it gently before trusting it fully, and always keep a hand near it during use so you can manage it manually if it doesn't grip as expected. Learning to tie and test a prusik correctly is one of the most genuinely valuable, low-risk skills a non-technical outdoorsperson can add, since it applies to self-rescue on a fixed line as much as to helping someone else.

sections.heading: Human Chains, Tag Lines, and Safe Low-Angle Assists
sections.body: Not every rescue assist needs rope hardware at all, and some of the safest options for non-technical helpers avoid it entirely. A human chain — a line of people, each braced and holding the hand or wrist of the next, anchored at one end to something solid or to a person firmly braced on stable ground — can extend reach across a short gap, a fast-moving shallow stream, or an unstable slope without ever putting a single person's full weight on an untested system, as long as everyone stays in contact with solid footing and no one commits their whole body weight to the chain. A tag line — a simple rope held from shore or solid ground and given to someone who's stable but needs a hand of reassurance or balance across a short obstacle — works the same way: it's a point of contact and confidence, not a load-bearing rescue system, and should never be treated as strong enough to hold a genuine fall or full body weight without backup. The common thread across all of these low-angle techniques is that they work by keeping everyone's feet on solid ground and never asking a single point of failure to hold a life. If at any point an assist would require someone to be fully suspended, unable to self-arrest, or dependent on a single rope or grip with no backup, that's the signal the situation has crossed from a safe low-angle assist into something that needs trained technical rescue.

sections.heading: Improvised Litters: Moving an Injured Person Without a Rope System
sections.body: Often the actual need isn't a rope system at all but simply moving an injured person a short distance to safety, and this can frequently be done without any rigging. A rigid door, a wide board, or a stretcher improvised from two sturdy poles threaded through the sleeves of two or three jackets zipped closed can carry someone a short distance on relatively flat, low-angle ground with four or more people carrying, spaced evenly and moving in step on command from one designated leader. Before moving anyone with a suspected spinal, neck, or serious fracture injury, the general guidance is to avoid moving them at all unless there's an immediate life threat like fire, rising water, or structural collapse that makes staying in place more dangerous than the move itself — improvised litter carries are for stabilized injuries and safe terrain, not a substitute for careful spinal precautions. On any slope, keep the litter level and carry the person's head slightly uphill unless a specific injury dictates otherwise, and never attempt to carry a litter down anything steep enough to require your own hands for balance — that's a technical lowering situation, not a carry. Communicate constantly during any litter carry: a single leader calling steps and hazards out loud keeps the whole team moving together rather than each person reacting individually to uneven ground.

sections.heading: Edge Protection and the Small Mistakes That Cut Ropes
sections.body: A surprising number of rope failures in both trained and improvised rescue settings come down to one overlooked detail: a rope running under tension across a sharp or rough edge — a rock lip, a window sill, exposed rebar, the corner of a vehicle — can be cut or badly abraded in a matter of seconds, especially if there's any movement or 'sawing' motion as the load shifts. This is true even of rope rated for far more static force than the situation requires; edge damage isn't primarily about the rope's strength rating, it's about a small contact area concentrating enormous pressure and friction on a single point. Whenever a rope must cross an edge under load, pad it — a folded jacket, a section of carpet, a pack, tarp material, anything that spreads the contact area and cushions the rope — and reposition the anchor or route if a clean padded path isn't achievable. Beyond edges, inspect any rope pressed into improvised service for obvious damage before trusting it: a fuzzy or flat spot on the sheath, a soft or lumpy section suggesting core damage, or any rope that's been exposed to chemicals, extreme heat, or UV degradation for a long period are all reasons to treat it as compromised rather than load-bearing. A rope that's already questionable for one of these reasons should be reserved for a tag line or non-critical use, not for anything a person's weight depends on.

sections.heading: When to Stop and Wait for a Trained Team
sections.body: There's a clear set of signals that mean the situation has moved past what an improvised, non-technical rescue should attempt, and recognizing them early is more valuable than any rigging skill. If the situation is genuinely high-angle — a person's full weight would need to hang from the system rather than simply steady them — that's a trained-team situation. If you don't have a verified solid anchor, or the only anchor options are questionable, that's a trained-team situation. If the person is unconscious, has a suspected spinal injury, or otherwise can't cooperate with their own rescue, the margin for error in any improvised system drops sharply and professional equipment and technique matter far more. If you find yourself building a compound or unfamiliar system under time pressure, without having practiced it beforehand in a low-stakes setting, that unfamiliarity is itself a hazard. In almost every one of these cases, the better use of your time is establishing contact with the person if it's safe to do so, keeping them calm and as stable as possible, calling for help immediately and giving dispatch a precise location and description of the terrain, and staying available to assist a trained team once they arrive rather than attempting the technical piece yourself. Waiting feels passive in a genuine emergency, but a slower, correctly executed professional rescue reliably beats a faster one that fails partway through.

guides.title: Structural Collapse: Self-Rescue, Void Awareness, and Helping Without Becoming a Casualty
guides.summary: Most deaths after a building collapse happen in the hours that follow the initial event, not during it. This guide covers what to do if you're trapped, how search teams find people in rubble, why secondary collapse is the single biggest threat to bystanders, and what an untrained civilian can safely do at a collapse site.

sections.heading: The First Minutes After a Collapse: What Kills People Next
sections.body: The structural failure itself — an earthquake bringing down a building, a gas explosion, a construction failure — is only the first hazard. What follows kills more people than most expect: secondary or progressive collapse of already-weakened structural members, fires ignited by ruptured gas lines or damaged electrical systems, dust inhalation and crush injuries going untreated, and untrained bystanders entering unstable debris and becoming additional casualties rather than rescuers. If you're near a structure that has just partially or fully collapsed, the immediate priority is getting clear of it and staying clear until it's been assessed, because aftershocks, settling debris, and structural members that were holding by a thread can fail minutes or even hours after the initial event with no warning. If you can see or hear anyone trapped, do not rush toward the debris pile — take a moment to look for obvious secondary hazards first: sagging or leaning sections that haven't fully come down, visible gas smell, sparking wires, smoke, or water pooling in ways that suggest a broken main. Call emergency services immediately, even if you plan to help while waiting, since professional urban search and rescue (USAR) resources take time to mobilize and every minute of advance notice matters. The instinct to rush in is natural and admirable, but the data on collapse-site casualties consistently shows that untrained rescuers moving too fast, without assessing the structure first, become a meaningful share of the injuries in the hours after a collapse.

sections.heading: If You're Trapped: Conserve Air, Protect Your Airway, Signal Smart
sections.body: If you find yourself trapped in debris, the first priority is protecting your airway — cover your nose and mouth with clothing, a mask, or even a cupped hand to filter dust, since collapse dust is a serious inhalation hazard on its own and can worsen breathing in a confined space. Avoid unnecessary movement that stirs up more dust or risks shifting unstable material around you; assess whether you can safely move at all before attempting it, and if movement risks further collapse or you're wedged in a way that seems stable, staying still is usually safer than struggling. Conserve your energy and, if applicable, your air supply by staying calm and limiting exertion and shouting to short, deliberate bursts rather than continuous yelling, which burns oxygen in a confined space and exhausts your voice quickly. If you have a phone with any signal or a working flashlight, use it, but also prepare a non-electronic backup: tapping on a pipe, a wall, or debris with something hard produces a sound that carries much farther through structural material than a shout does and doesn't run out of battery. A steady rhythm — three taps, pause, three taps — is more likely to be recognized as an intentional signal by search teams than random noise, echoing the same rule-of-three principle used in surface signaling. Whistle if you have one; it carries farther than a voice and costs almost no energy to use repeatedly.

sections.heading: The Call-and-Listen Search Pattern: How Rescuers Find Voices in the Rubble
sections.body: Urban search and rescue teams commonly work debris piles using a call-and-listen technique: all equipment, machinery, and unnecessary talking on site is stopped for a short period, a searcher calls out loudly — sometimes with a specific repeated phrase such as calling into a gap or void and identifying themselves as a rescue team — and then everyone present goes completely silent and listens for any response: a voice, a tap, a scrape, anything. This is repeated systematically across a grid of the debris field, because sound travels unpredictably through broken structural material, and a response that's inaudible from one spot may carry clearly from a position a few meters away. This is exactly why, if you're trapped, your best chance of being heard is often not during the noisy, active phase of a search but during these deliberate silent listening windows — which is one more reason to conserve your voice and energy for short, repeated signals rather than continuous shouting that might miss the exact moment someone is listening. If you're a bystander helping at a site before trained teams arrive, you can use a simplified version of this same technique yourself: stop everyone talking and moving, call out clearly, then go completely silent and listen for several seconds before moving to the next spot, rather than shouting continuously while people around you are also making noise.

sections.heading: Understanding Void Spaces
sections.body: A void is any open, unfilled space that forms within collapsed debris, and these are the pockets that keep people alive in a collapse — and the primary target of a systematic search. Voids commonly form next to large, rigid objects that resist crushing: staircases, structural beams and columns, large pieces of furniture like a sturdy desk or dresser, bathtubs, and door frames, which is precisely why 'get near something solid and rigid' is a durable piece of collapse-survival guidance in the moment a structure is actually coming down around you, distinct from and in addition to the standard drop-cover-hold-on response taught for earthquakes specifically. Search teams prioritize probing near these features first because statistically, that's where survivable voids are most likely to exist, rather than searching randomly across an entire debris field with equal attention everywhere. If you're trapped in or near a void, resist any urge to try to enlarge it yourself by pushing or clearing debris unless you're confident it's safe to do so — debris resting in a stable arch or wedge configuration can be holding weight that would otherwise collapse further onto you, and removing the wrong piece can bring the space down rather than open it up. Voids can also trap dangerous gas buildup or dust concentrations, which is another reason airway protection matters even once you know you're in open space rather than fully crushed.

sections.heading: Secondary Collapse: The Biggest Threat to Untrained Helpers
sections.body: Secondary or progressive collapse — additional structural failure after the initial event — is consistently identified as the leading cause of injury and death among untrained bystanders and even some professional responders at collapse sites, and it's exactly what makes acting fast and acting carefully feel like they're in tension. A structure that has partially failed can have remaining members holding enormous, unevenly distributed loads that were never designed for the damaged configuration; a beam that looks intact may be one aftershock, one gust of wind, or one shifted piece of debris away from letting go completely. Removing a single piece of debris that looks like simple clutter can also be the one thing holding a larger section in place, a phenomenon trained USAR teams specifically train to recognize and avoid through careful, incremental removal rather than pulling material out quickly. This is why professional collapse response always begins with a structural size-up — an assessment of what's still standing, what's likely to move, and what load paths remain — before anyone enters, and why untrained bystanders are consistently advised against entering a collapsed or partially collapsed structure at all, no matter how urgent the need to reach someone inside feels. If someone can be reached and helped from outside the structure's footprint without entering it, that's overwhelmingly the safer option compared with going inside, even briefly.

sections.heading: Reading a Damaged Structure Before You Go Near It
sections.body: A handful of visible signs reliably indicate a structure is actively unstable and should not be approached, even by someone trying to help. Visible leaning of walls or entire sections out of vertical, floors or roof lines that sag or bow noticeably, cracks that are new, widening, or running diagonally across a wall in a stair-step pattern through masonry joints, dust still actively sifting down from ceilings or upper floors, and audible creaking, cracking, or popping sounds are all signals that the structure is still moving or settling, not that it has finished failing and stabilized. Similarly, a structure with visible fire, smoke, or a strong gas odor, exposed and possibly live electrical wiring, or standing water that could be masking a washed-out foundation should be treated as off-limits until utilities are confirmed shut off and professionals have assessed it. None of these signs require engineering training to recognize — they're deliberately simple, visible cues that CERT and other civilian preparedness programs teach specifically because they don't require expertise to apply, just attention and the discipline to act on what you see rather than override it with urgency. If a structure shows any of these signs, the correct response is the same as with a downed power line or a chemical spill: keep a safe distance, keep others back too, and report the specific hazard to responders as soon as you can reach them, rather than working around it.

sections.heading: What Untrained Civilians Can Safely Do
sections.body: There is a meaningful, genuinely useful role for untrained bystanders at a collapse site, and it doesn't require entering unstable structures. From outside the structure's footprint, you can call out and listen using the same call-and-listen technique professional teams use, and report anything you hear or see — a voice, a tap, a visible limb or piece of clothing — with as precise a location as you can describe, since that single piece of information can direct a professional team's search far faster than a blind systematic sweep. You can help clear light, loose surface debris that's clearly not load-bearing — broken glass, loose boards, small rubble — from areas where injured people have already been extracted, freeing up space for medical treatment and further extraction work, as long as you stay well clear of anything that looks structural or load-bearing. You can provide basic first aid to people who've already been freed, using the same triage and bleeding-control principles covered in the First Aid guide, which is often more urgently needed than additional hands on the debris pile itself. You can also serve as a runner, relaying information between people at the scene and arriving responders, or help organize bystanders into a calm, coordinated group rather than a chaotic crowd, which measurably improves outcomes at real disaster scenes. None of this requires entering a compromised structure, and all of it directly helps.

sections.heading: What NOT to Do Around a Collapsed Structure
sections.body: Do not enter a collapsed or visibly damaged structure to search for people, no matter how personal or urgent the motivation, unless you have specific training and equipment for it — this bears repeating because it's the single most common and most dangerous mistake bystanders make. Do not remove debris quickly or by pulling on the nearest visible piece; if you're clearing debris at all, it should be from a stable exterior area, worked slowly, one piece at a time, watching for any shift or settling as material is removed. Do not use open flame, smoke, or operate anything that could spark near a site where a gas leak is possible or unconfirmed. Do not assume a structure that survived the initial event is now stable — many progressive collapses happen specifically because a damaged structure held briefly before failing further. Do not climb onto a debris pile to get a better vantage point or to try to see or reach someone, since debris piles shift under added weight in ways that are impossible to predict from the surface. Do not ignore your own exhaustion, dehydration, or injuries while trying to help others — a helper who collapses or is injured becomes one more person needing rescue, diverting resources from the people already trapped. And do not block access routes with vehicles, crowds, or equipment; arriving professional teams need clear paths in and out more than they need extra hands at the debris pile itself.

sections.heading: Marking and Communicating With Professional Responders
sections.body: Professional USAR teams use a standardized structure and hazard marking system — commonly a spray-painted square or X near an entry point — to communicate search status between teams and shifts without needing to re-search ground someone has already covered. A single diagonal slash typically marks that a team has begun searching a structure; a completed X or filled-in marking indicates the search of that structure is finished, often with quadrants noting which team searched it, when, and how many living or deceased victims were found and removed. If you're at a scene before professional teams arrive and you search or clear an area yourself, leaving a simple, clear written note at the entry point — your name or group, the time, and what you found or didn't find — helps arriving teams avoid wasting time re-covering ground you've already checked, exactly the same principle behind the official marking system, just in plain language. When professional responders do arrive, the most useful thing you can do is hand off information concisely and immediately: exactly where you heard or saw someone, what hazards you noticed, what's already been checked, and how many people are known to be missing or accounted for. Resist the urge to over-explain or relive the experience in the moment — responders need the operational facts fast, and a calm, organized handoff measurably speeds up what happens next.

sections.heading: CERT and Preparing Before Disaster Strikes
sections.body: Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) programs exist specifically to close the gap this guide describes: they're free or low-cost courses, widely available through local emergency management agencies in many countries, that train ordinary residents in exactly the skills covered here — structural size-up basics, safe light search and rescue technique, cribbing and simple leverage methods for lifting light debris off a person without entering an unstable structure, basic triage using the START method to prioritize care among multiple injured people, fire suppression basics, and disaster psychology for staying functional and helping others stay calm under stress. The training deliberately does not teach entering heavily damaged structures or attempting technical rescues — it teaches the judgment to recognize when a situation is within safe civilian capability and when it isn't, reinforcing the exact boundary this guide has emphasized throughout. Beyond formal training, practical preparation includes knowing how to shut off gas and water utilities at your own home if it's ever safe to do so, keeping a basic kit with work gloves, a dust mask or respirator, a flashlight, and a whistle accessible rather than buried in storage, and having a family or household plan for where to meet if a structure becomes unsafe to re-enter. The people who handle a real collapse situation most effectively are consistently the ones who already knew, calmly and in advance, exactly where the line sits between helping and becoming one more person who needs to be found.
